## Learning Objectives

Explain what "proportional hazards" means.

## Lesson

With the Cox proportional hazards model,
we assume that if you fix $t$,
one hazard rate is a constant multiple of the other.
In other words, the hazard rates are always proportional to each other.

Suppose we have two groups, group 1 and group 2.
Let $h_1(t)$ and $h_2(t)$ be the hazard rates of groups 1 and 2, respectively,
at time $t$.
The proportional hazards assumption is that $h_2(t) = c h_1(t)$,
where $c$ is a positive constant.

I'd like to look at what this means for the survival curve,
but in order to do so, I have to introduce a new function.
The "cumulative hazard" in group 1 is
$$
\Lambda_1(t) = \int_0^t h_1(s)\,ds \text{.}
$$
You don't need to memorize this;
it's just an interim step between the hazard and the survival function.
What you need to know is that
$$
\Lambda_1(t) = -\log S_1(t) \text{,}
$$
where $S_1(t) = P(T_1 > t)$.
If you don't believe me, you can check out the proof in the callout below.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Caution: Math

First, note that
$$
\begin{align*}
\frac{d}{ds} \log S(s) &= \frac{1}{S(s)} \frac{d}{ds} S(s) & \text{chain rule} \\
&= \frac{1}{S(s)} \frac{d}{ds} \left(1 - F(s)\right) & \text{definition of cumulative distribution function} \\
&= \frac{1}{S(s)} \left(-f(s)\right)  & \text{definition of probability distribution function} \\
&= - \frac{f(s)}{S(s)} \text{.}
\end{align*}
$$
Next,
$$
\begin{align*}
\Lambda(t) &= \int_0^t h(s)\,ds \\
&= \int_0^t \frac{f(s)}{S(s)} \,ds \\
&= \int_0^t \left(-\frac{d}{ds} \log S(s)\right) \,ds \\
&= - \int_0^t \frac{d}{ds} \log S(s) \,ds \\
&= - \log S(t) \text{.}
\end{align*}
$$




:::

Now we can connect the hazards to the survival functions.
Proportional hazards means
$$
\begin{align*}
h_2(s) &= ch_1(s) \\
\int_0^t h_2(s)\,ds &= \int_0^t ch_1(s) \,ds \\
\int_0^t h_2(s)\,ds &= c \int_0^t h_1(s) \,ds \\
\Lambda_2(t) &= c\Lambda_1(t) \\
-\log S_2(t) &= -c\log S_1(t) \\
-\log S_2(t) &= -\log S_1(t)^c \\
S_2(t) &= S_1(t)^c \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
$$
So, at any time $t$, we can get the survival probability
for group 2 by raising the survival probability for group 1 to the power $c$.

## Problems

### Problem 1

True or false:
Proportional hazards is equivalent to proportional survival.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

False.
Proportional hazards is equivalent to $S_2(t) = S_1(t)^c$,
not $S_2(t) = c S_1(t)$.

:::
